extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, economists, manufacturers, and readers interested in intellectual property and industrial policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles about patents, copyright, export controls, excise regulation, and the economic effects of granting/withdrawing monopolies in manufacturing (illustrated by the bobbin-net trade). Useful for assessing patent policy and its industrial consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and basic form of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are exclusive privileges granted to the first introducers to encourage the importation, improvement, or invention of machines and discoveries relating to manufactures; they are granted on payment of certain fees for terms varying from five to twenty years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms and expenses differ by country (table provided). Patents are intended to encourage invention by granting exclusive use for a limited term in exchange for disclosure and fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term should allow inventor to recoup investment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of importance to preserve to each inventor the sole use of his invention, until he shall have been amply repaid for the risk and expense to which he has been exposed, as well as for the talent he has exerted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should aim to provide sufficient exclusive use to reward risk and creativity while balancing public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative difficulty: varying merit and drafting problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties in the degree of merit among inventions are numerous, and the difficulties of legislating on patents are great; it is almost impossible to frame a law not open to serious objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should recognize that a one-size-fits-all patent law may produce practical objections and require careful balancing of competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent enforcement and judicial defense difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty of defending an English patent in any judicial trial is very great; recorded instances in which the defence has succeeded are comparatively few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak or costly enforcement reduces the practical value of patents and should be accounted for when designing patent systems and when evaluating patent worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial strategies when enforcement is weak
rubrics_metrics.description: Some manufacturers, not regarding a patent as securing a monopoly price, sell the patent article at a price producing only ordinary profits of capital so that no competitor can derive profit from invading the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pricing patented products to discourage profitable infringement can be an alternative to expensive litigation; inventors may choose defensive commercial strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright law compared to patent law
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright is allied to patents; those species of property that require the highest talent were late to be recognized. Means of deciding literary infringement are not difficult, but present law can cause hardship and impede advancement of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing intellectual property regimes, consider differences in ease of adjudication and potential negative effects on dissemination of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excise licensing and prescriptive production rules deter experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: For revenue purposes manufacturers are often obliged to take out a license and to work according to certain rules and make stated quantities at each operation; when these quantities are large, they deter manufacturers from making experiments upon new materials and prevent discovery by trial of improved methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue-driven regulatory requirements can hinder innovation; exemptions or tailored rules may be needed to avoid stifling experimental activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental exemptions must be limited and vetted
rubrics_metrics.description: Permission has been obtained for fit persons to make experiments without excise interference, but if frequently granted it might be abused; the greatest protection is bringing public opinion to bear and judging by the public character of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators granting experimental exemptions should apply vetting (e.g., applicant reputation) and limit frequency to prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider smuggling when imposing heavy duties or prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy duties or prohibitions are ineffective as well as injurious because, unless articles excluded are very large, there arises a price at which they will be clandestinely imported by smugglers; the extent to which smuggling can be carried should be considered in imposing duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade restrictions should be designed with realistic assessment of enforcement limits and smuggling incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of removing monopolies (patent expiry or abandonment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal of a monopoly can have important effects: widespread adoption of machines, speculative mania for acquiring machines, rapid increase in machine-making orders, fall in prices from over-supply, disappointment and ruin for many early speculators, and subsequent technical improvements that devalue older machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patent monopoly ends, anticipate rapid market entry, diffusion of production, downward price pressure, and social consequences for small owners and workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market diffusion dynamics after monopoly removal
rubrics_metrics.description: After patents/monopolies are removed, machines may be rented or bought (often by instalments), novices pay for instruction, machine-makers can be overwhelmed with orders, and wages for certain trades (e.g., machine-making smiths) can temporarily rise due to demand for skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers and firms should plan for training needs, credit/finance issues, and temporary wage distortions accompanying rapid diffusion of technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity-improving machines can depress small owners and wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction and multiplication of more powerful machines must depreciate the value of existing smaller machines, tend to sink small owners into journeymen, and either greatly increase labour or depress workmen's wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical progress, while increasing output, can create distributional harms; anticipate displacement and consider measures to ease transition for small owners and workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on labor mobility are counterproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws forbidding workmen to leave the country were ineffective and contrary to liberty; they deterred return more than migration and failed to prevent disguised departures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies restricting worker movement are both ethically problematic and practically ineffective; alternatives should be sought to address concerns about skill transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export prohibitions on machinery trade off maker vs user interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting export of machinery was justified as preventing foreigners using improved machinery to compete, but in practice it sacrifices the interests of machinery makers for those who use machinery; removing prohibition may increase makers' numbers and intelligence and foster growth of the machine-making industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering export controls on machinery, weigh the benefits to domestic makers (innovation, industry growth) against the desire to limit foreign competition; restrictions may impede a growing class of more intelligent machinery makers.
